newsitem.title: USA: Nobel economics winner Vickrey dies after award.
newsitem.headline: Nobel economics winner Vickrey dies after award.

text.p: Nobel prize winning economist William Vickrey died on Friday three days after he won the prestigious award, saddening colleagues at Columbia University where he had laboured for six decades.

Columbia, where Vickrey was a professor emeritus of economics, said that according to police the 82-year-old scholar died after suffering a heart attack at the wheel of his car. He was driving to Boston for a conference of a group he founded, TRED (Taxation, Resources, Economics and Development).

The Canadian-born Vickrey, a follower of British economist John Maynard Keynes and a believer that balanced budgets harm the economy, shared the 1996 Nobel Prize for Economic Science with James Mirrlees, 60. Both men, who have never met, were cited for "their fundamental contributions to the economic theory of incentives." The $1.2 million prize was the biggest since the prize was first awarded in 1969.

Columbia's president, George Rupp, said according to police Vickrey was found slumped behind the wheel of his car late on Thursday night on a highway near his home in upstate New York and pronounced dead at a hospital early on Friday morning.

Rupp said Vickrey "has been an inspiration to students and faculty at Columbia University for more than 60 years both because of the brilliance of his extraordinarily active mind and because of his deep concern for other human beings.

"Those of us who knew Bill Vickrey and those who met him for the first time this week celebrated the recognition that the Nobel Prize brought him and now we join together to mourn his death," Rupp added. "It is our hope that the work of this dedicated and important scholar will continue to be given the worldwide attention it attracted this week."

Vickrey and Mirrlees won the prize on Tuesday for their separate contributions "to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information." The research of both focused on how organisations could make competent decisions based on incomplete -- or asymmetric -- information.

Vickrey spent his career crusading for innovative solutions to common economic problems of taxation, utilities and urban transportation. His latest cause was a campaign against balancing the federal budget.

In an interview with Reuters shortly after winning the award, Vickrey said balancing the federal budget would cripple the U.S. economy, sending unemployment soaring to 15 percent and bringing on a stock market crash.

Instead, federal policy-makers should gradually raise the deficit to about $500 billion from the $126 billion estimated for the current fiscal year, he said, in order to boost purchasing power and get unemployment to below one percent.

The current unemployment rate of 5.2 percent, Vickrey said, arrests Gross Domestic Product at about 12 percent below its potential and isolates the poorest members of society in an economic wasteland of joblessness and crime.

His comment drew a scathing rebuttal from Speaker of the House of Representatives Newt Gingrich, who said, "Now we know that he is an obsolete socialist, representing all the values that collapsed with the Berlin Wall."

Vickrey politely refuted Gingrich's "socialist" label, calling himself a follower of Keynes. He said his work on the ill effects of balancing the budget was "my most important piece of work at the moment."
A common theme running through much of his work is "congestion pricing," the notion that free market forces can influence consumers' use of roadways, air traffic corridors and phone lines.

In 1959, he proposed a solution for easing gridlock in Washington, D.C. -- electronically assessing road user fees. The fees should rise gradually to peak at times of highest demand, thus discouraging congestion, Vickrey said.

Vickrey was born in Victoria, British Columbia, in 1914 but moved to New York State when he was very young. He received his undergraduate degree from Yale University and did his graduate studies at Columbia.
